title: Your AI chat isn't a diary

beats: She used an AI chatbot like a diary. Then deputies showed up at her door.
Here's what's reported. On September twenty-sixth, a Florida woman allegedly wrote that she'd "shoot up" a sheriff's office. The next day, a message allegedly mentioned a new gun.
Anthropic says it monitors chats for threatening content. Serious flags can go to a human reviewer. Here, the team decided to report it to police.
September thirtieth: a felony charge, for a written threat of a mass shooting under Florida law. Arraignment is set for November second. It's an allegation, not a conviction.
Is this the first time? No. Reports say at least two other chats reached police since August. San Antonio, a man arrested. San Francisco, no charges.
And it's not just one company. OpenAI has said chats about harming others can go to human reviewers, and imminent threats may go to police.
Anthropic's privacy policy, effective September tenth, allows disclosure when it believes that's reasonably necessary to prevent serious harm.
Look closer at its transparency report: zero emergency requests from police in late twenty twenty-five. But it doesn't count reports the company makes on its own.
The sheriff's line: what you share with AI is "never truly anonymous." What we don't know: how often chats get flagged, or the exact messages.
So: a chatbot isn't a diary. Does that make you safer, or watched? Tell me below. Follow for the next AI story.
